samples.summary: The sign-out erase is enforced only in the tab that performed it; a second tab with the document open re-writes the content to disk afterwards, defeating "signing out leaves nothing behind" on a shared device
samples.evidence:
`eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` (offline-erase.ts:236) calls `denyOfflineWrites(who)`, which adds to `const erased = new Set<string>()` at offline-erase.ts:120 — documented as "In memory only, and deliberately". `dropAllForUser` likewise marks `evictedKeys`, a module-level Map (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:174-190) whose own comment concedes it is "Still tab-local". Nothing about the erase is visible cross-tab: it does not touch `wafflebase-offline-persistence` (the one preference `isPersistenceEnabled` reads through `getOfflinePersistenceEnabled()`, which IS cross-tab via the `storage` event), and writes no localStorage flag another tab consults.

Attack/failure chain, on the exact shared-device threat model the design names: user has doc D open in tabs A and B. In tab A they click Log out. `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout` deletes every row for that user. Tab B's `DurableYorkieProvider` is still mounted, and its `isPersistenceEnabled: () => getOfflinePersistenceEnabled() && isOfflineWritePermitted(userId)` (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx) evaluates true in tab B's realm — the preference is untouched and tab B's `erased` set is empty. Tab B's next `appendChange` finds no header, so `refuseIfEvicted` consults tab B's own (empty) `evicted` set and returns a silent success, and tab B's SDK then writes a fresh full snapshot on its next compaction via `saveSnapshot`, which is unconditionally permitted. The user's document content is back on the disk they just signed out from, and nothing runs again to remove it — tab B eventually 401s into `logout({eraseLocalData:"none"})`, which by design erases nothing. Retention is then bounded only by the 30-day sweep, which requires some account to return to that browser.

Not currently reachable because `supportsClientKey()` gates the durable path on `@yorkie-js/react >= 0.7.23` and packages/frontend/package.json:66 pins `0.7.22`; per the task doc the dependency bump is "the whole remaining action — no code here changes with it", so this arms on a version bump alone.

samples.summary: The per-device client-key salt is shared by every account on the browser profile and never rotated, so it does not defend against the co-tenant of a shared profile it is otherwise scoped for
samples.evidence: `deviceSecret()` (durable-session.ts:137) reads one `wafflebase-durable-device` value for the whole origin, and `durableClientKey` (line 96) composes `wb:{secret}:{userId}:{docKey}`. The doc comment at lines 80-94 states the salt exists because "Yorkie authorizes `ActivateClient` and `DeactivateClient` on token validity alone", so a derivable key lets anyone with any valid token tear down another member's per-document client. On a shared browser profile — the case this whole feature is written around — user B can read the same localStorage value, and `userId` (sequential member id) and `docKey` (`sheet-<id>` from the URL) are the public ingredients the comment already names, so B can derive A's client keys for any document id B can guess and deactivate them with B's own token. Nothing clears or rotates the secret on logout: `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout` (offline-erase.ts:236) removes documents and the identity mirror but never `DEVICE_SECRET_KEY`, and `resetDeviceSecretForTest` (line 157) is test-only.

samples.summary: `randomSecret()` falls back to `Math.random()` for a value the module documents as an unguessability control
samples.evidence: durable-session.ts:117-126: when `crypto.getRandomValues` is absent the loop fills the 8 bytes with `Math.floor(Math.random() * 256)`. `Math.random()` is not a CSPRNG and its state is recoverable from a handful of outputs in common engines, so a secret minted on that branch is not unguessable — which is the single property the salt is there to provide (lines 80-94). The inline comment argues the branch is unreachable because `navigator.locks` and `crypto` are both secure-context APIs, but that is an assumption about the runtime rather than an enforced precondition, and nothing in `supportsDurableSession()` (line 57) checks for `crypto`. Failing closed (declining durability when no CSPRNG is available) would be strictly safer than minting a weak secret.

samples.summary: `collectStale` sweeps archives across every account on the device unscoped, destroying another account's only copy of unreconcilable work — and leaves the `onlyUser` guard written for exactly this case unused
samples.evidence: wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1190 calls `this.dropArchivesWhere(BY_ARCHIVED_AT, range)` with no third argument. `dropArchivesWhere`'s own doc comment (lines 1300-1304) says `onlyUser` exists precisely because "an archive holds a whole document, so a sweep over `archivedAt` alone would delete another account's on a shared device" — and no caller ever passes it, so the parameter is dead and the stated protection is not applied. `OfflineRuntime` runs `store.collectStale()` once per session (offline-runtime.tsx), so any signed-in account destroys every other account's archives older than 30 days. By this feature's own design an archive is the only copy of work the SDK could not reconcile with the server, so this is cross-account destruction of unrecoverable data. The behaviour is argued for in the design doc, but the contradiction between the guard's documentation and its non-use should be resolved one way or the other.

samples.summary: The route-param traversal test's per-request encoding assertion was relaxed from universal to existential, so an unencoded id in a companion request can now pass
samples.evidence: Before this change every request URL a call site produced had to satisfy `expect(pathname).toContain(encodeURIComponent(TRAVERSAL))`. url.test.ts:170-174 replaces that with `paths.some(...)`, so one encoded request now vouches for all siblings. The surviving per-URL check (line 163) only rejects paths that normalize to exactly `/auth/logout`, which is a function of how deep the raw id is interpolated: `TRAVERSAL = "../../auth/logout"` (line 68) lands on `/auth/logout` from `${BASE}/documents/${id}` but not from a deeper route such as `${BASE}/workspaces/${slug}/members/${id}`. A future multi-request call site that interpolates an id without `seg()` at such a depth would therefore pass both assertions. The change is motivated by `deleteWorkspace`'s new `fetchDocuments()` companion request (workspaces.ts:127); a narrower fix — asserting the universal property only over URLs that name the route under test — would keep the coverage.

samples.summary: An expired session leaves full document content on the device indefinitely, and the durable client keeps writing more of it under the now-invalid identity
samples.evidence: auth.ts:134 skips `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` when `eraseLocalData === "none"`, which is what the 401 arm of `fetchWithAuth` passes (auth.ts:~277). Session expiry is the commonest way a session ends on the shared/borrowed machine this feature is explicitly designed around, and on that path nothing is erased and no pending erase is recorded. Compounding it, `collab-document-provider.tsx` keeps a `lastKnown` identity ref and uses `person = me ?? lastKnown.current`, so after `fetchMeOptional` starts answering `null` the durable client stays mounted and continues persisting the document under the expired user's store scope. The only remaining collectors are the 30-day sweep and the per-session revocation reconcile, both of which need some account to return to that browser. The trade-off (not destroying the un-pushed change log on an event the user did not choose) is argued in the design, but the residual is unencrypted document content retained past the end of authorization, with no bound the user can see or act on.

samples.summary: `documentIdsIn` fails open: when the workspace lookup fails and the route param is a slug, the workspace-deletion purge silently drops nothing, leaving content past the end of the authority to read it
samples.evidence: workspaces.ts:101-115 resolves the ref with `fetchWorkspace(ref).catch(() => undefined)` and then filters on `document.workspaceId === ref || (!!workspace && document.workspaceId === workspace.id)`. Callers pass the `/w/:workspaceId/...` route param, which the app navigates with the *slug*, while `document.workspaceId` is always the id — so if `fetchWorkspace` fails (offline, transient 5xx, a 403 on a workspace being deleted) the filter matches nothing and `purgeOfflineDocuments(doomed, { dropArchives: true })` at line 136 is handed an empty array. `deleteWorkspace` then reports success while every local copy and archive of that workspace's documents stays on disk, including archives that `recoverOfflineCopy` will later re-materialize as documents the user owns. The design's stated rule is that content must not outlive the authority to read it; the per-session `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` reconcile is the backstop, so the exposure is bounded by one session rather than unbounded.

verdict.reason: Every element of the claim verifies against the repo. `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout` (offline-erase.ts:236-256) records the denial only in the module-local `erased` set (offline-erase.ts:120-125), and `dropAllForUser` marks only the erasing tab's `evictedKeys` entry (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:173-189, 1083-1110) — the file's own comment concedes it is "Still tab-local". No cross-tab signal exists: grep across packages/frontend/src finds `storage` listeners only in offline-persistence-preference.ts:95,104 and date-format-preference.ts:79, and nothing watches `wafflebase-offline-user` (offline-erase.ts:54) or broadcasts a logout. A second tab's durable client therefore still evaluates `isPersistenceEnabled` true (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:172-173), its post-erase append hits the empty `evicted` set and returns a silent success (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:653-656, 711-720), and its next `saveSnapshot` — gated only by `refuseIfDisabled` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:580-581, 382-391) — writes a fresh full snapshot of the document back to disk after sign-out. api/auth.ts:277 confirms the eventual 401 path erases nothing. I considered refuting on `already-guarded` via `supportsClientKey()` (yorkie-capabilities.ts:76-82 vs the 0.7.22 pin at packages/frontend/package.json:66), which does make the durable path unmountable in this build (collab-document-provider.tsx:223,342-347); but that is a feature-wide build capability gate, not a guard on this hazard, and accepting it would void every finding about this feature. The defect is real and in-lane (sensitive data remanence on the shared-device threat model the design names).
